source.title: Persistent Representational Misalignment Induces Vision-Language Model Failures
source.authors: Yonatan Gideoni; Yoav Gelberg; Tim G. J. Rudner; Yarin Gal

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling, truncation, or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly challenges strong cross-modal representational convergence, combining similarity-structure and analogy measurements with a paired-data generalization test. It is a challenge/refinement rather than a reproduction of the original scale-alignment method.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports held-out-concept generalization results and associations between alignment and VLM benchmark performance; these are included where they test functional alignment or its relation to capability. Cited results from other work are not recorded. Hyperparameter search values are not results on the claim.
record.test_reason: The paper argues that a strong cross-modal Platonic convergence fails. It shows this with its own measurements: COCO image/caption similarity structures (CosSimRMSE ratios), VisLingA analogy retrieval in vision versus text models, and a held-out-concept test of whether trained vision-to-language adapters generalize. These bear directly on V2, V4 and V7. It does not run a scale sweep of cross-model alignment.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that vision and language representations are linearly unalignable because the modalities carry different information, so misalignment should persist regardless of scale or adapter complexity. They say this disproves a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, while weaker partial-alignment versions likely hold, as the weak scale trend in Figure 2 suggests. They also argue the misalignment causes a predicted held-out-concept generalization failure and correlates with VLM failure benchmarks. They note that fixing alignment has not been shown to reduce failures and that alignment may be only one cause.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce the original Platonic Representation Hypothesis scale-alignment experiment. It uses cosine-similarity RMSE, analogy retrieval, paired-data omission tests, and a mutual-nearest-neighbours alignment measure for a benchmark correlation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured discrepancy varies across image/caption examples and model pairings. The authors report that changing the large-scale image-filtering threshold from 0.25 to 0.2 yielded accuracies around half those in Table 2, suggesting sensitivity to filtering and possible data leakage.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 37 LLaVA models with different ViT-B backbones, vision/language mutual-NN alignment correlates with accuracy on VLM-failure benchmarks (0.38–0.72), but not with reasoning controls (0.05–0.07).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Greater cross-modal representational alignment between backbones predicts fewer VLM failures on perception/grounding benchmarks.

record.problems: The paper states that representational similarity has no universally agreed definition and that its measures are not exhaustive. Most failure-benchmark evidence is correlational, and the authors say they do not directly show that fixing misalignment reduces failures. Cross-modal alignment is not tracked through a controlled scale-and-performance sweep. Large-scale held-out detection may be affected by data leakage or longer completions; the authors report that lowering the image-filter threshold reduced accuracy to around half the Table 2 values.
record.rows_left_out: No separately stated results relevant to the tested versions were omitted. Model-specific analogy values and exact point estimates from Figure 2 are not tabulated in the text, so only the text's aggregate statements and stated trend are recorded.

untested.parts: No scale-or-capability sweep of alignment between independently trained models. The within-modality cross-objective gaps (r4, r5) are single snapshots.
No controlled measurement of cross-modal alignment as both models scale. Only a weak, unquantified scale trend in vision-model analogy accuracy (r14).
Seeds and same-architecture reinitializations are not studied.
Stitching layers, relative representations and unpaired mapping are not tested. Mapping loss on in-distribution concepts is not reported.
No universal neurons, SAE features or circuits.
The study does not vary similarity metrics or their settings (e.g. k in mutual-NN), and no OOD input comparison of alignment scores is made.

Plateauing with scale is not measured. Whether shared data or objectives explain convergence is not isolated; the authors instead attribute misalignment to inherent differences in information content between the modalities.

missing.what: In Figure 2, CLIP text encoders are the worst language models and CLIP vision encoders the best vision models on analogies. The authors attribute this to cross-modal supervision pulling each encoder toward the other modality, which bears on V7's shared-objective cause.
Large-scale models prompted to name only the main object (≤8 tokens) reach 19.6% held-out detection.
With the image filter threshold at 0.2 instead of 0.25, large-scale held-out accuracies fall to about half of Table 2, suggesting leakage.

record.verdict_notes: V6 links are removed throughout because no metric, setting or input choice is varied. The V1 label is dropped: there is no cross-model scale sweep, and the weak vision-scale trend concerns cross-modal analogy agreement (V2). The V7 links on the held-out-concept rows are dropped because those rows test whether the learned map generalizes (V4), not what causes convergence. Comparator and baseline rows (r2, r10, r13, r23, r26, r29) are reference values, not results. The Figure 5 correlations are figure-only and recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly track representational similarity between independently trained models across a controlled scale-and-performance sweep.
Does not measure alignment increasing as both component models independently improve or scale; Section 5 holds the language model fixed while varying vision backbones.
No comparison of same-architecture models trained from different initializations or analysis of shared subspaces across seeds.

Does not test stitching layers, relative representations, or alignment without paired data; its functional test uses adapters trained on paired data, and its theoretical/empirical argument concerns concept-preserving linear maps.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified or compared.
Does not systematically sweep similarity-measure settings such as neighbour count or evaluate convergence out of distribution.
Does not isolate shared pretraining objectives or establish that shared data/objectives explain representational alignment. Its paired-data intervention concerns functional generalization.
